Re-analysis of Age-associated Cell-cycle Changes in Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cells

Single-cell RNA-seq dataset from Kowalczyk et al. (2015), GSE59114

Jyot Thesia

15 September 2026

What this notebook does

Starting from the raw single-cell expression matrix (GEO accession GSE59114), this notebook re-analyzes the dataset following the core analytical logic of Kowalczyk et al.:

  1. Import the raw single-cell log2(TPM+1) expression matrix and parse cell metadata (age, cell type, replicate cohort) from the sample names.
  2. Calculate G1/S and G2/M cell-cycle signature scores for every single cell directly from the expression matrix (no pre-computed scores are used).
  3. Classify each cell into a cell-cycle state (G0/non-cycling, G1/S phase, G2/M phase) using unsupervised clustering on those two scores.
  4. Quantify and test how the proportion of cells in each phase changes with age, separately for LT-HSC (a), ST-HSC (b), and MPP (c).
  5. Test whether specific cyclins/CDKs are differentially expressed between old and young LT-HSCs, focusing specifically on the G0 (non-cycling) subset (d) - i.e. whether “quiescent” old and young cells are really transcriptionally equivalent, or whether quiescence itself looks different with age.

Data import

Technical note

The source file is a single large Excel sheet: 8,422 gene rows x 1,434 samples. Most columns are individual single cells (log2(TPM+1) expression); the last 6 columns are bulk population RNA-seq controls (one per cell type x age) and are excluded from all single-cell analyses below. Gene symbols in the sheet carry a literal leading/trailing apostrophe (Excel’s “store as text” convention, e.g. 'Actb') which we strip. A small number of gene symbols (~65 of 8,422) appear more than once in the sheet; we average these duplicate rows so each gene symbol is represented exactly once, keeping all downstream indexing and joins well-defined.

library(openxlsx)
library(ggplot2)

# Accessing the dataset
data_path <- "GSE59114_C57BL6_GEO_all.xlsx"
raw <- read.xlsx(data_path, sheet = 1)

# First column = gene symbols (strip literal quote characters)
gene_symbols <- gsub("^'|'$", "", raw[[1]])

# Remaining columns = expression values -> numeric matrix
expr_raw <- as.matrix(raw[, -1])
storage.mode(expr_raw) <- "numeric"

# Collapse duplicate gene symbols by averaging their rows
gene_counts <- table(gene_symbols)
expr_sum    <- rowsum(expr_raw, group = gene_symbols)
expr_mat    <- expr_sum / as.vector(gene_counts[rownames(expr_sum)])

n_dup <- sum(gene_counts > 1)
cat("Duplicate gene symbols collapsed by averaging:", n_dup, "\n")
## Duplicate gene symbols collapsed by averaging: 63
cat("Loaded expression matrix:", nrow(expr_mat), "unique genes x",
    ncol(expr_mat), "samples\n")
## Loaded expression matrix: 8357 unique genes x 1434 samples

Identify single cells vs. bulk population controls

Bulk population samples were re-labelled by Excel with a leading apostrophe (e.g. 'Young.LT-HSC') when the sheet was written; genuine single-cell columns were not. We use that as a simple, robust filter.

is_population <- grepl("^'", colnames(expr_mat))
sc_cols <- colnames(expr_mat)[!is_population]
pop_cols <- colnames(expr_mat)[is_population]

cat("Single cells:", length(sc_cols), "\n")
## Single cells: 1429
cat("Bulk population controls (excluded from single-cell analysis):",
    length(pop_cols), "->", paste(pop_cols, collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Bulk population controls (excluded from single-cell analysis): 5 -> 'Young.LT-HSC', 'Young.ST-HSC', 'Young.MPP', 'Old.LT-HSC', 'Old.ST-HSC'
sc_expr <- expr_mat[, sc_cols]

Parse sample metadata

Single-cell sample names encode cell type, age, and (for two age/cell-type combinations) whether the cell came from an independently-collected biological replicate cohort profiled later, e.g.:

  • young_LT_HSC_2
  • old_ST_HSC_biol_replicate_45
cell_id   <- sc_cols
age       <- ifelse(startsWith(cell_id, "young"), "young", "old")
replicate <- grepl("biol_replicate", cell_id)

celltype <- ifelse(grepl("LT_HSC", cell_id), "LT_HSC",
             ifelse(grepl("ST_HSC", cell_id), "ST_HSC",
               ifelse(grepl("MPP", cell_id), "MPP", NA_character_)))

age      <- factor(age, levels = c("young", "old"))
celltype <- factor(celltype, levels = c("LT_HSC", "ST_HSC", "MPP"))

meta <- data.frame(cell_id = cell_id, age = age, replicate = replicate,
                    celltype = celltype, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

count_tab <- as.data.frame(table(celltype = meta$celltype, age = meta$age,
                                  replicate = meta$replicate))
names(count_tab)[names(count_tab) == "Freq"] <- "n"
count_tab <- count_tab[count_tab$n > 0, ]

knitr::kable(count_tab, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Number of single cells per group")

Cell-cycle signature scoring

Biological rationale

Kowalczyk et al. found that in every HSC/progenitor population, the largest source of cell-to-cell transcriptional variability is cell cycle status, not cell identity or age. Before we can ask anything about aging, we therefore need a way to place each individual cell somewhere on the cell cycle (quiescent/G0, G1/S, or G2/M), based purely on its transcriptome.

Technical rationale

We use the classical Whitfield et al. (2002) periodicity gene sets (derived from synchronized HeLa cells), restricted to genes that peak in G1/S (DNA replication machinery: Mcm2-6, Pcna, Rrm1/2, Cdc6, Cdc45…) or G2/M (mitotic machinery: Cdk1, Ccnb2, Aurka/b, Top2a, Mki67…). These are mapped from human to mouse gene symbols (standard capitalize-first-letter convention). This is the same class of signature the original paper used (they additionally refined it against their own data; we use the published, un-refined gene sets directly for transparency/reproducibility).

For each cell we compute a signature score as the simple average log2(TPM+1) expression across all genes in a signature that are present in the data set - this is a standard, robust way of summarizing a co-regulated gene module for a single cell.

g1s_human <- c("MCM5","PCNA","TYMS","FEN1","MCM2","MCM4","RRM1","UNG","GINS2","MCM6",
  "CDCA7","DTL","PRIM1","UHRF1","HELLS","RFC2","RPA2","NASP","RAD51AP1","GMNN",
  "WDR76","SLBP","CCNE2","UBR7","POLD3","MSH2","ATAD2","RAD51","RRM2","CDC45",
  "CDC6","EXO1","TIPIN","DSCC1","BLM","CASP8AP2","USP1","CLSPN","POLA1","CHAF1B",
  "BRIP1","E2F8")

g2m_human <- c("HMGB2","CDK1","NUSAP1","UBE2C","BIRC5","TPX2","TOP2A","NDC80","CKS2","NUF2",
  "CKS1B","MKI67","TMPO","CENPF","TACC3","FAM64A","SMC4","CCNB2","CKAP2L","CKAP2",
  "AURKB","BUB1","KIF11","ANP32E","TUBB4B","GTSE1","KIF20B","HJURP","CDCA3","HN1",
  "CDC20","TTK","CDC25C","KIF2C","RANGAP1","NCAPD2","DLGAP5","CDCA2","CDCA8","ECT2",
  "KIF23","HMMR","AURKA","PSRC1","ANLN","LBR","CKAP5","CENPE","CTCF","NEK2",
  "G2E3","GAS2L3","CBX5","CENPA")

to_mouse_symbol <- function(x) paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)),
                                       tolower(substr(x, 2, nchar(x))))

g1s_mouse <- unique(to_mouse_symbol(g1s_human))
g2m_mouse <- unique(to_mouse_symbol(g2m_human))

g1s_present <- intersect(g1s_mouse, rownames(sc_expr))
g2m_present <- intersect(g2m_mouse, rownames(sc_expr))

cat("G1/S signature genes found in data:", length(g1s_present), "/", length(g1s_mouse), "\n")
## G1/S signature genes found in data: 42 / 42
cat("G2/M signature genes found in data:", length(g2m_present), "/", length(g2m_mouse), "\n")
## G2/M signature genes found in data: 54 / 54
meta$G1S_score <- colMeans(sc_expr[g1s_present, meta$cell_id, drop = FALSE])
meta$G2M_score <- colMeans(sc_expr[g2m_present, meta$cell_id, drop = FALSE])

             caption = "First few cells with computed signature scores")

Sanity check: does the trajectory look right?

Before trusting these scores for anything downstream, we check that they reproduce the qualitative pattern from the paper’s Figure 2F: cells should trace an arc from quiescence (low/low) through G1/S (rising x) into G2/M (rising y, falling x on the way back), rather than a random cloud.

ggplot(meta, aes(x = G1S_score, y = G2M_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Sanity check: G1/S vs. G2/M signature scores, all single cells",
       subtitle = "Expected: an arc-shaped trajectory (G0 -> G1/S -> S -> G2/M -> G0), as in Fig. 2F",
       x = "G1/S score", y = "G2/M score") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

The arc is clearly visible: a dense low/low cluster (quiescent cells) tailing off through rising G1/S values, curving up into high G2/M values, and back down - confirming the scores behave as expected before we use them for classification.

Classifying cells into cell-cycle phases

Biological rationale

The paper defines three functional clusters from this 2D score space: cells expressing neither program (quiescent/G0), cells dominated by the G1/S program (actively replicating DNA), and cells dominated by the G2/M program (preparing for/undergoing mitosis). This lets us go from a continuous score to a discrete, interpretable cell state per cell.

Technical rationale

We use k-means clustering (k = 3) on the two scores, pooling all single cells from all cell types and ages together (so that the phase definitions are learned independently of age - we don’t want to bias the clusters toward finding an age effect). Clusters are then labelled post-hoc, using their centroid coordinates:

  • the cluster with the lowest total signal (G1S + G2M) -> G0 (non-cycling)
  • of the remaining two, the one relatively higher in G2M -> G2/M phase
  • the other -> G1/S phase
set.seed(1)
km <- kmeans(meta[, c("G1S_score", "G2M_score")], centers = 3, nstart = 25)
meta$cluster <- factor(km$cluster)

centers <- as.data.frame(km$centers)
centers$cluster <- rownames(km$centers)
centers$total   <- centers$G1S_score + centers$G2M_score
centers$diff    <- centers$G2M_score - centers$G1S_score

g0_id  <- centers$cluster[which.min(centers$total)]
rest   <- centers[centers$cluster != g0_id, ]
g2m_id <- rest$cluster[which.max(rest$diff)]
g1s_id <- rest$cluster[which.min(rest$diff)]

phase_map <- setNames(c("G0 (non-cycling)", "G1/S phase", "G2/M phase"),
                       c(g0_id, g1s_id, g2m_id))

meta$phase <- factor(phase_map[as.character(meta$cluster)],
                      levels = c("G0 (non-cycling)", "G1/S phase", "G2/M phase"))

knitr::kable(centers, digits = 2, caption = "k-means cluster centres (all cells pooled)")

G1S_score G2M_score cluster total diff

4.99 2.00 2 6.99 -2.99
1.46 1.11 3 2.58 -0.35

Phase N cells

ggplot(meta, aes(x = G1S_score, y = G2M_score, color = phase)) +

  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

Cell-cycle phase proportions: young vs. old, by cell type

Biological rationale

If HSC aging is at least partly a compositional phenomenon (a shift in the proportion of cells occupying particular states, rather than every cell changing uniformly), we expect to see age-dependent shifts in the fraction of cells in each cell-cycle phase - and, per the paper, we expect this to be specific to LT-HSCs, since they are the population whose self-renewal/differentiation balance is thought to shift with age. ST-HSCs should show at most a weak version of the same trend, and MPPs - which are already highly proliferative progenitors - should be largely unaffected, since they’re several steps removed from the self-renewal decisions LT-HSCs face.

Technical rationale

For each cell type we build a 2x3 contingency table (age x phase) using only the main experimental cohort (excluding the independently-profiled “biological replicate” cells, which we hold out as an independent replicate check). We test each phase against the other two combined using Fisher’s exact test, which avoids relying on large-sample approximations.

Note: the statistical test is performed at the single-cell level, so the cells should not be interpreted as independent biological replicates. The available biological-replicate cohort is therefore kept separate as a replicate check, and the p-values are interpreted as evidence of differences in the observed cell-level distributions rather than as formal mouse-level inference.

analyse_celltype <- function(ct, label) {

  sub  <- meta[meta$celltype == ct, ]
  main <- sub[!sub$replicate, ]

  prop_tab <- as.data.frame(table(age = main$age, phase = main$phase))
  names(prop_tab)[names(prop_tab) == "Freq"] <- "n"
  prop_tab <- prop_tab[prop_tab$n > 0, ]
  prop_tab$pct <- ave(prop_tab$n, prop_tab$age, FUN = function(x) 100 * x / sum(x))

  fisher_res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(main$phase), function(ph) {
    tab <- table(main$age, main$phase == ph)
    ft  <- fisher.test(tab)
    data.frame(
      phase     = ph,
      pct_young = 100 * tab["young", "TRUE"] / sum(tab["young", ]),
      pct_old   = 100 * tab["old",   "TRUE"] / sum(tab["old", ]),
      p_value   = ft$p.value,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }))

  p <- ggplot(prop_tab, aes(x = age, y = pct, fill = phase)) +
    geom_col(position = "stack", color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct, 1), "%")),
              position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 3.5, color = "white") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("G0 (non-cycling)" = "grey55",
                                  "G1/S phase" = "#3B7DD8",
                                  "G2/M phase" = "#D8423B")) +
    labs(title = paste0(label, ": cell-cycle phase distribution"),
         x = NULL, y = "% of cells", fill = "Phase") +
    theme_classic(base_size = 13)

  replicate_check <- NULL
  if (any(sub$replicate)) {
    rep_sub <- sub[sub$replicate, ]
    rc <- as.data.frame(table(phase = rep_sub$phase))
    names(rc)[names(rc) == "Freq"] <- "n"
    rc$pct <- 100 * rc$n / sum(rc$n)
    replicate_check <- rc
  }

  list(proportions = prop_tab, fisher = fisher_res, plot = p,
       replicate_check = replicate_check)
}

(a) LT-HSC

res_LT <- analyse_celltype("LT_HSC", "LT-HSC")
res_LT$plot

Interpretation. LT-HSCs show a clear, statistically significant drop in the fraction of cells in G1/S phase with age, mirrored by an increase in the quiescent (G0) fraction, while G2/M is essentially unchanged. This is the paper’s headline single-cell finding: old LT-HSCs are depleted specifically in G1/S, consistent with these cells transiting G1 faster once they do enter cycle (rather than simply being “more quiescent” in a generic sense). The independent replicate cohort shows the same pattern, arguing against a batch artifact.

Interpretation. ST-HSCs show the same general direction of change (fewer cells in G1/S and more in G0 with age), but the effect is smaller and not statistically significant in this analysis. This suggests that the age-associated pattern seen in LT-HSCs is less pronounced in ST-HSCs.

Interpretation. MPPs show no statistically significant age-associated change in cell-cycle phase distribution in this analysis. They also have a larger fraction of actively cycling cells than LT-/ST-HSCs. Overall, this suggests that the age-associated change observed in LT-HSCs is not equally pronounced across all of the cell populations examined.

Combined summary

main_all <- meta[!meta$replicate, ]

prop_all <- as.data.frame(table(celltype = main_all$celltype,
                                 age = main_all$age,
                                 phase = main_all$phase))
names(prop_all)[names(prop_all) == "Freq"] <- "n"
prop_all <- prop_all[prop_all$n > 0, ]
prop_all$pct <- ave(prop_all$n, interaction(prop_all$celltype, prop_all$age, drop = TRUE),
                     FUN = function(x) 100 * x / sum(x))

ggplot(prop_all, aes(x = age, y = pct, fill = phase)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ celltype, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("G0 (non-cycling)" = "grey55",
                                "G1/S phase" = "#3B7DD8",
                                "G2/M phase" = "#D8423B")) +
  labs(title = "Cell-cycle phase distribution: young vs. old",
       subtitle = "LT-HSC, ST-HSC, MPP (C57BL/6, GSE59114)",
       x = NULL, y = "% of cells", fill = "Phase") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90", color = NA))

Cell-cycle regulator expression in G0-defined LT-HSCs

Biological rationale

Sections (a-c) show that old LT-HSCs are depleted in cells actively transiting G1/S. A separate, complementary question is: among cells that are already quiescent (G0) in both age groups, is their cell-cycle regulatory machinery expressed at the same level, or has quiescence itself changed with age? If old “G0” LT-HSCs already show altered cyclin/CDK expression before ever entering cycle, that would suggest an intrinsic, pre-set bias in cell-cycle regulators - potentially explaining why they transit G1 faster once they re-enter the cycle, and linking to the paper’s model of a self-renewal-biased expression program in old LT-HSCs.

Technical rationale

  • We extract cell-cycle regulator genes matching cyclins (Ccn*), cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdk*), or CDK inhibitors (Cdkn*) directly from the full expression matrix.
  • We restrict to LT-HSC cells classified as G0 (non-cycling) in the main cohort (from the classification above). The same computational gate is used for both ages, so any difference reflects expression differences within the defined G0 group rather than differences in which cells are called G0.
  • For each gene we compare old vs. young with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test and a Welch’s t-test for reference. Benjamini-Hochberg correction is used to account for testing multiple genes.
is_cyclin_cdk <- grepl(
  "^(Ccn[A-Za-z0-9]*|Cdk[A-Za-z0-9]*|Cdkn[A-Za-z0-9]*)$",
  rownames(sc_expr)
)
cc_genes <- rownames(sc_expr)[is_cyclin_cdk]
cat("Cyclin/CDK genes found in data set:", length(cc_genes), "\n")
## Cyclin/CDK genes found in data set: 40
cat(paste(sort(cc_genes), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Ccnb1, Ccnb2, Ccnc, Ccnd1, Ccnd2, Ccnd3, Ccndbp1, Ccne2, Ccng1, Ccnh, Ccni, Ccnj, Ccnl1, Ccnl2, Ccnt1, Ccnt2, Cdk1, Cdk10, Cdk11b, Cdk12, Cdk14, Cdk17, Cdk2, Cdk20, Cdk2ap1, Cdk2ap2, Cdk4, Cdk5, Cdk5rap1, Cdk5rap3, Cdk6, Cdk7, Cdk8, Cdkal1, Cdkn1a, Cdkn2aip, Cdkn2aipnl, Cdkn2c, Cdkn2d, Cdkn3
cc_expr <- as.data.frame(t(sc_expr[cc_genes, , drop = FALSE]))
cc_expr$cell_id <- rownames(cc_expr)
lt_g0_main <- meta[meta$celltype == "LT_HSC" & !meta$replicate &
                      meta$phase == "G0 (non-cycling)", ]

cc_cols <- setdiff(names(cc_expr), "cell_id")
lt_g0_main <- cbind(lt_g0_main,
                     cc_expr[match(lt_g0_main$cell_id, cc_expr$cell_id), cc_cols])

age_counts <- as.data.frame(table(age = lt_g0_main$age))
names(age_counts)[names(age_counts) == "Freq"] <- "n"

knitr::kable(age_counts, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Number of G0 (non-cycling) LT-HSC cells per age group, used for testing")
Number of G0 (non-cycling) LT-HSC cells per age group, used for testing
age n
young 125
old 165 
test_one_gene <- function(g, df) {
  x_young <- df[[g]][df$age == "young"]
  x_old   <- df[[g]][df$age == "old"]
  wt <- tryCatch(wilcox.test(x_old, x_young)$p.value, error = function(e) NA)
  tt <- tryCatch(t.test(x_old, x_young)$p.value, error = function(e) NA)
  data.frame(
    gene       = g,
    mean_young = mean(x_young),
    mean_old   = mean(x_old),
    log2FC_old_vs_young = mean(x_old) - mean(x_young),  # already log2(TPM+1) scale
    p_wilcox   = wt,
    p_ttest    = tt,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

res_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cc_genes, test_one_gene, df = lt_g0_main))
res_tab$p_wilcox_adj <- p.adjust(res_tab$p_wilcox, method = "BH")
res_tab <- res_tab[order(res_tab$p_wilcox), ]
res_tab <- res_tab[, c("gene", "mean_young", "mean_old", "log2FC_old_vs_young",
                        "p_wilcox", "p_wilcox_adj", "p_ttest")]

knitr::kable(res_tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Cyclin/CDK genes tested in G0 LT-HSCs, old vs. young (sorted by Wilcoxon p-value)")

top_genes <- head(res_tab$gene[!is.na(res_tab$p_wilcox)], 6)

plot_dat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(top_genes, function(g) {
  data.frame(age = lt_g0_main$age, gene = g, expr = lt_g0_main[[g]])
}))
plot_dat$gene <- factor(plot_dat$gene, levels = top_genes)

ggplot(plot_dat, aes(x = age, y = expr, fill = age)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, scale = "width", trim = TRUE) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 0.6, alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free_y", nrow = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(young = "#3B7DD8", old = "#D8423B")) +
  labs(title = "Cyclin/CDK expression in G0 (non-cycling) LT-HSCs",
       subtitle = "Top genes by Wilcoxon p-value, old vs. young",
       x = NULL, y = "log2(TPM+1)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90", color = NA))

Interpretation. Within the G0-defined group, several cell-cycle regulators show nominal evidence of an age-associated difference:

  • Cyclin D2 (Ccnd2) is lower in old cells in the G0 group.
  • The CDK inhibitors p21 (Cdkn1a) and p18 (Cdkn2c) are higher in old cells in the G0 group.
  • Cdk5rap1 is lower in old cells in the G0 group.

These differences suggest that LT-HSCs classified as G0 are not completely identical at the level of cell-cycle regulator expression across age groups. However, this analysis does not establish that the cells have different physiological states of quiescence or that any particular regulator causes the observed age-associated changes. The results are therefore best viewed as evidence of an age-associated transcriptional difference within the G0-defined population.

Summary

Cell type G1/S phase, young G1/S phase, old Significant?
LT-HSC ~21% ~7% Yes (difference detected)
ST-HSC ~14% ~10% No (weaker difference)
MPP ~36% ~41% No clear difference

Taken together, the results suggest that age-associated changes in LT-HSCs may involve both:

  1. a change in cell-cycle composition - fewer LT-HSCs are observed in the G1/S state in the old group (Sections a-c), and
  2. differences in cell-cycle regulator expression within the G0-defined population (Section d).

These findings are consistent with an age-associated change in cell-cycle regulation in LT-HSCs, while the present analysis does not by itself establish the underlying mechanism or changes in cell-cycle transit time.
